title: A computational framework for principally polarized abelian varieties and applications
authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos, Etienne Piasecki, and Benjamin Wesolowski
abstract:
We construct a new framework for cryptographers to work with principally polarized abelian varieties (PPAVs).
This framework offers a computational approach to abelian varieties agnostic to the choice of a coordinate system, culminating in the definition of an efficient model for principally polarised abelian varieties. We exhibit an instantiation of our framework by means of the theta model, thereby streamlining the documented capacities of the model, and extending them with new fundamental algorithms, like the computation of automorphism groups. Our framework focuses on what can be done with these objects, computationally, while relegating low-level considerations to the background, like the specific choice of a coordinate system (and thus the necessity to rely on Mumford's theory of theta coordinates).
We illustrate the utility of our framework by proving that we can interpolate polarised isogenies in any dimension, generalizing to higher dimensions the most disruptive algorithm for elliptic curves in recent years. We prove that this interpolation offers a universal, canonical, and compact way to represent isogenies.

      Abstract. We construct a new framework for cryptographers to work
      with principally polarized abelian varieties (PPAVs). This framework of-
      fers a computational approach to abelian varieties agnostic to the choice
      of a coordinate system, culminating in the definition of an efficient model
      for principally polarised abelian varieties. We exhibit an instantiation of
      our framework by means of the theta model — thereby streamlining
      the documented capacities of the model, and extending them with new
      fundamental algorithms, like the computation of automorphism groups.
      Our framework focuses on what can be done with these objects, compu-
      tationally, while relegating low-level considerations to the background,
      like the specific choice of a coordinate system (and thus the necessity
      to rely on Mumford’s theory of theta coordinates). We illustrate the
      utility of our framework by proving that we can interpolate polarised
      isogenies in any dimension, generalizing to higher dimensions the most
      disruptive algorithm for elliptic curves in recent years. We prove that this
      interpolation offers a universal, canonical, and compact way to represent
      isogenies.


Keywords: Isogeny-based cryptography · Principally polarized abelian vari-

1   Introduction

In recent years, the substantial investment into building large scale quantum
computers has resulted in increased interest in post-quantum cryptography.
Isogeny-based cryptography is a promising candidate for constructing protocols
that are secure in the presence of classical and quantum adversaries. Since its
inception, the field has primarily focused on isogenies between elliptic curves.
Indeed, though some protocols were constructed using the higher dimensional
generalisation of elliptic curves (namely, principally polarised abelian varieties,
or PPAVs) [7, 14, 17], they were mostly deemed to be of limited practical interest.
    This changed in 2022 when a wave of results [6, 22, 30] broke one of the most
well-established isogeny-based protocols in the field at that time: SIDH/SIKE [13],
a key exchange mechanism. Remarkably, these attacks brought new life to the
field. At a high-level, the attacks showed how to efficiently interpolate isogenies:

on a sufficiently large torsion basis, one can recover the connecting isogeny.
   This has proven to be a powerful constructive tool as it allows us to embed
an isogeny of elliptic curves of large degree into an isogeny of smoother degree
between higher dimensional abelian varieties. As a consequence of this break-
through result, we now have a new way to represent isogenies; it is the first
representation that can describe non-smooth isogenies between any two elliptic
curves. With impressive strides towards optimising the computation of higher
dimensional isogenies [9, 11], this new representation is efficient.
    Higher dimensional isogenies are now an indispensable tool in constructing
isogeny-based cryptosystems. Using this new representation of isogenies, exist-
ing protocols have been dramatically improved. Most notably, the recent two-
dimensional variants of SQIsign, the only isogeny-based candidate in the NIST
post-quantum cryptography standardisation process, are faster, smaller, and rely
on more well-understood security assumptions. New protocols, which rely on this
interpolation result, have also been constructed (see, for example, [2, 3, 4, 18]).
    Despite their new-found importance, higher dimensional objects remain elu-
sive to a wider audience. Moving beyond dimension one introduces new complex-
ities, requiring a strong background in algebraic geometry. The current state of
affairs is unwelcoming, focused on low-level coordinate systems, and impractical
for the design higher level algorithms.

and perfectly suited for the development of low-level algorithms and implemen-

applications. Consider, for example, computing a (polarised) isogeny of degree ℓ

dimension g > 2, the situation is far murkier, and the cryptographer who wants
to justify an isogeny computation needs to jump through a series of hoops. Al-
gorithms for computing isogenies between PPAVs of general dimension g were
developed primarily by Cosset, Lubicz, and Robert using the theory of theta

represented in the theta model of level n. This model is crucial for the design of
the algorithm, but makes its subsequent use difficult: even parsing the input and
output requires heavy Mumford-machinery, and the task itself is generally only
presented as a ‘change-of-level’ algorithm, to be paired with Mumford’s isogeny
theorem to obtain the desired algorithm. In addition to this, though the work
by Lubicz and Robert in 2023 [21] is the current state-of-the-art and is usually
the cited reference, they assume that the degree of the isogeny is coprime to
n. Usually we take even level n, thus ruling out computations of even degree
isogenies. One must trace back the citations to find an algorithm in [20] that
work for all degrees (coprime to the characteristic of the field).

   Instead of jumping through these hoops, it is tempting to use PPAVs as a
black box, but the state-of-the-art is missing the appropriate interface.


Contributions. The goal of this paper is to construct a new framework for
cryptographers to work in higher dimensions. We offer a computational approach
to abelian varieties agnostic to the choice of a coordinate system, culminating in
the definition of an efficient model for principally polarised abelian varieties. This
definition focuses on what can be done with these objects, computationally, in
simple yet unambiguous language, without relying on highly abstract notions like
Mumford’s theory of theta coordinates. We then prove that in this framework,
one can generically construct algorithms for more advanced functionalities, like
computing the characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism.
     Furthermore, we exhibit an instantiation of our framework by demonstrating
that the level-4 theta model is such an efficient representation. This is done by
reframing classical results on the theta model within our framework, and by
providing new algorithms expanding the documented capabilities of this model.
In particular, we prove that in this theta model, one can efficiently compute the
automorphism group of a PPAV.
     Finally, to show the utility of our framework, we use it to prove that we can
interpolate (polarised) isogenies in any dimension, generalizing to higher dimen-
sions the most disruptive algorithm for elliptic curves in recent years [6, 22, 30].
This generalisation was suspected soon after the case of dimension 1 [33], and
the general structure of the algorithm (Algorithm 6) is indeed very similar. Yet,
the lack of a systematic notion of an efficient model for the objects at play have
impeded early attempts at proving this result. It was not clear whether some of
the key ingredients were available in higher dimension (in particular, the com-
putation of automorphism groups). Thanks to our framework, the interpolation
algorithm Algorithm 6 can be expressed in clear and precise language, and it
applies not only to the level-4 theta model, but also to any future instantiation
of our framework.
     We furthermore show that isogeny interpolation provides a universal, canon-
ical, and compact way to represent isogenies, in the following sense: given any
efficient representation of an isogeny, one can compute interpolation data for this
isogeny that is compact (i.e., of length poly-logarithmic in its degree), canonical
(i.e., only depends on φ and not on how it is encoded), and this interpolation data
itself constitutes an efficient representation of φ (e.g., it allows one to evaluate
φ on any input).


Related work. The theta model has been the standard way to computation-
ally manipulate abelian varieties since Robert’s thesis [32]. This seminal work
demonstrated how Mumford’s theory of theta functions provides an explicit co-
ordinate system for PPAVs, where points are effectively described by projective
coordinates and isogenies by rational maps. Subsequent literature expanded the
library of efficient algorithms for this theta model, and applications emerged,
4          Maria Corte-Real Santos, Etienne Piasecki, and Benjamin Wesolowski

always with one major downside which the present work aims to address: its
understanding requires a mastery of advanced notions of algebraic geometry.
    The most noteworthy attempt at cataloguing the capabilities of the theta
model has certainly been the lecture notes [16, Section 2.1]. In particular, some
of the properties of the theta model listed in [16, Theorem 2.1.1] are axioms
required in our definition of an efficient model — this has proved valuable in our
proof that the theta model is indeed an efficient model.
    One can see [16] as a first step towards making the computational theory of
PPAVs more accessible, although it is still focused on one particular coordinate
system: the theta model (unlike our framework which is agnostic to the under-
lying machinery — the theta model is only one possible instantiation). In the
same vein, the article [12] presents an alternative perspective on the theta model
from a more combinatorial point of view, meant to be more accessible.


Structure of the paper. The paper is structured as follows:

    – Section 2 presents some background material, including a gentle introduction
      to PPAVs. We emphasize that the framework developed in this article is
      meant to be usable without extensive background in algebraic geometry.
      The material introduced in Section 2 is useful to understand the semantics
      of the model or for actually instantiating it (e.g., with the theta model).
    – In Section 3, we develop the core of the new framework: the notion of effi-
      cient models for principally polarized abelian varieties. Starting with Defi-
      nition 3.1, the rest of the section presents the list of computational axioms.
    – In Section 4, we prove some results that hold generically in any instantia-
      tion of the model. They help in designing more advanced algorithms (like
      the interpolation algorithm). In particular, we prove how to compute the
      characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism, or the norm of an isogeny.
    – In Section 5, we introduce the theta model, and in Section 6 prove that our
      framework can be instantiated by this model. More precisely, we prove that
      the theta model satisfies all the properties of an efficient models for PPAVs,
      except one: the canonical and compact form for N -isogenies. We call such a
      model a proto-efficient model. Note that while our framework is designed to
      be usable without extensive background in algebraic geometry, instantiating
      it does require familiarity with the underlying theory; in particular, these
      two sections require much more technical background.
    – In Section 7, we prove the isogeny interpolation theorem (Theorem 7.1): in
      any proto-efficient model for PPAVs, given an integer N and the images of
      enough points through an N -isogeny, one can recover the isogeny in polyno-
      mial time. As an application, we deduce that any proto-efficient model can
      be enhanced into an efficient model for PPAVs (Theorem 7.5). In particular,
      the theta model is an efficient model (Corollary 7.7).

2     Background
The aim of this section is to give a brief introduction to abelian varieties in any
dimension, focusing on the aspects that are relevant to our work. We emphasize
that the goal of this article is to give the reader the tools to work with abelian
varieties for cryptography without needing an extensive background in algebraic
geometry. As such, we do not claim to give a full treatment of the theory of
abelian varieties; for a more in-depth introduction we refer a reader to [24]. In
fact, our computational framework introduced in Section 3 can be used without
even understanding much of the algebraic geometry discussed in the present
section. The present section is useful to understand the semantics of the model
(what are binary strings meant to represent?), or for actually instantiating the
framework (as in Section 6 where we prove that the theta model is an efficient
model).

2.1   The geometry of abelian varieties
An abelian variety X of dimension dim(X) = g is a smooth projective algebraic
variety of dimension g which is also an algebraic group, namely it has a group law
+ : X × X → X, such that + and its inverse − are morphisms of varieties. We
denote by 0X the identity element of X. We will only consider abelian varieties
defined over Fp .

2.2    Principally polarised abelian varieties
In cryptography, we often take for granted that we have equations defining our
elliptic curves in projective space. For instance, every elliptic curve can be rep-
resented by a Weierstrass equation. In contrast, for higher dimensional abelian
varieties, we no longer have nice models to work with in general. Hidden under
the surface is the fact that the existence of equations for elliptic curves stems
from the existence of a canonical principal polarisation. This fails in higher di-
mension: some abelian varieties have no principal polarisation, and others have
more than one (so we need to be careful with our choice). To alleviate this is-
sue, we consider only principally polarised abelian varieties, a notion which we
explain in this section.

3   Efficient models for principally polarized abelian
    varieties

In this section, we introduce the notion of an efficient model for PPAVs. We
wish to represent PPAVs, points on PPAVs, and morphisms between PPAVs as
binary strings. Such strings correspond to sets Sppav , Spt , Smrph ⊂ {0, 1}∗ . The
notation X, P or φ will typically be used to denote a binary encoding of some
underlying PPAV X, point P or morphism φ.
    We then ask for algorithms to manipulate these encodings. For instance, an
algorithm A .isomorphic would take as input the encodings X, X ′ ∈ Sppav of
two PPAVs, and decide whether or not they are isomorphic. Another algorithm
A .torsion would take as input the encoding X ∈ Sppav of a PPAV and an
integer, and return the encodings Pi ∈ Spt of the N -torsion points of the variety.
With appropriate bounds on the length of encodings and on the complexity of
the family of algorithms A , we say that A is an efficient model for PPAVs, and
the elements of Sppav , Spt or Smrph are called efficient (A -)representations of
the underlying objects.
    While the intuitive idea is rather simple, making it precise requires a level of
formalism that can rapidly become cumbersome. In applications of this frame-
work, one would typically conflate a PPAV X with its binary representation X.
In contrast, to ensure that we build on solid ground, the present section carefully
distinguishes objects from their binary representation.

Definition 3.1 (Efficient model for PPAVs). Let A be a (probabilistic)
algorithm. Let Sppav ⊂ {0, 1}∗ be a set of binary strings, and let ppav be a
map ppav : Sppav −→ {(q, X) | X is a PPAV over Fq }. For any X ∈ Sppav
with ppav(X) = (q, X), let Spoint (X) ⊂ {0, 1}∗ be a set of binary strings,
and let ptX be a map ptX : Spoint (X) → X(Fp ). Let Smrph ⊂ {0, 1}∗ be
a set of binary strings, and let mrph be a (not necessarily surjective) mor-
phism mrph : Smrph −→ {φ | φ is a morphism between two PPAVs}. The tuple

3.1   Axioms on efficiency and encodings

In the one dimensional case, elliptic curves are typically represented by some
equation like the Weierstrass equation. The coefficients of the equation constitute
an encoding of the curve. We then have efficient algorithms to, for instance,
decide if two such equations define isomorphic elliptic curves. A point on a curve
is a solution of the equation, and its coordinates constitute an encoding of the
point. This encoding needs not be unique (for instance when using projective
coordinates), but can always be normalized to a “canonical” form. The following
definition captures these ideas and generalizes them to PPAVs.
